title: Funeral and parade tempo and the bass drummer's pacing
summary: He explains how beats and walking pace changed at funerals, how a bass drummer paces a long Lions Club parade, and why he prefers bass to snare.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, they're very fast, they're very fast today. There's a lot of difference, and then they're not, you see? There's something, you got to do it. Even you take the fumes, long years ago, I was playing fumes with Chris Kelly and Buddy and then they got the fumes more since the day, you play, you play, four beats still measure, but at that time you hit that bass, 12 hit one, and the stage on the four, three. The generator. That's the many players today, you see? Long years ago, they got one beat on that bass too. One, two, three, four.
Yeah, one, two, three, four. Why do you think they changed the style like that?
No, the style ain't changed, it's just a question they don't want to get under much quicker. They want to what?
They get under much quicker. They want to march a little faster.

A little faster. A little faster. A little faster. It won't take much time. It won't take much time. You take the snare drum player, and the minute they stop playing the fumes, you pick up one at a time. Then you get to the graveyard faster, because if you wouldn't do that, you'd be all, you'd need about one o'clock, it'd be nine o'clock at night before you get to the graveyard or something like that. I mean, it'd take you much longer, you know what I mean? So I mean that way they'd rush it on. In other words, you walk faster now? Yeah, well you walk faster. In the fumes you walk, yeah you walk a little bit faster, not too much faster, but you walk a little faster at them times, you know what I mean? And you take also in the street parading. If you can a parade down, you take like up there on Cornwall there from the Lions Club by the way, if you bass drum player and you know how to pick up on the time, you'd be all day long getting down there. You'd be two o'clock and you still wouldn't be the Canal Street. So you have to pick them up and care them while they're fresh, while they got that good walking spirit about them, you see? Well you can linger coming back. You want to get them down there the whole walk while you're fresh. Because if you linger along while you're fresh, when you're coming back, you're going to have to drag you back. So you got to bring them down there and bring yourself too while you're fresh. And then coming back, you know what I mean? You can take it easy. And then as you get after two o'clock you want to try to step them up again because the time is getting short. The 60 some odd blocks from the den, you try to get them back there before you get too tired, you see? Then them guys there start getting tired too and then they're full of juice and full of fun. Well they started slowing up too, you see? So the bands slow up and they're slow but by your, just keep them on going, you understand? They'll keep them on moving, they be moving, they be tired but they be still moving. Because if you don't do that, you're going to be running late. Last year we used to knock off at 6 o'clock. Last year at 5.30 we was done. I mean, I mean, guys was done, they had their fun, they was tired and it was a good thing we got them back because they kind of burned out their stuff. They didn't care about going no more, that was there no. When we got in the den that was it. They paid off and then for five minutes after six I was home. Which parade was that? The Lions Club. The Lions Club. I've been waiting up there for them for about six or seven years. They have a pretty good club, nice fellas to get along with. And they have two bands. You see, if you work with one band on the parade on the corner of the day, it might be a shorter run to further than you're going to know you play the parade with one band. You don't have no rest because every time you stop everybody has music, everywhere you pass. Music. You might just stop playing and you don't know whether you want to hear music. When you got two bands you relax for maybe three or four blocks or at least three blocks and the other band will give you a little relaxation, you understand? When you got that one band proposition, no sooner you stop you don't walk a block. Fellas are out of music and the snare drum player he's going to catch some sand because I do stop. But when he start he don't stop. When he, with that five minutes of whistle, seven minutes whistle blowing in the morning on the corner of the morning, he don't stop no more, that's him. Yeah, that's right. You got to beat the time because they want that more, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Them fellas want to march by that, you see? Well I'm relaxing, I'm walking for a couple of blocks of that bass drum on my shoulder, you see? But he don't have no rest. That's the end of him. That's one reason I got away from playing snare drum. A lot of fellas ask me not to play snare drum. I don't want to play no snare drum. I'd rather play the bass drum. Man, you'd rather have that bass drum. I say I got a light drum to catch, don't worry about it. Even though I have that thing on my shoulder every time. You understand? I do get a rest. But the guy with the snare drum, he don't get the motor. That's all. When you knock off, that's all he is.
